Quantum Reservoir Forecasting of S&P 500 Volatility — Diagnostic Report (1 October 2026), Annotated

Overview

This study forecasts next month's realized volatility (RV) of the S&P 500 and compares two quantum reservoir models (QR1, QR2) with ten classical benchmarks. Each quantum model is a simulated 10-qubit circuit: 7 input qubits receive one month of economic and market data, and 3 memory qubits carry information across the three most recent months (t−3, t−2, t−1). The circuit's couplings are random and fixed; only a linear readout on the measured qubit values is trained.

  • QR1 uses inputs RV, MKT, DP, IP, RV_q, STR, DEF and reads all 10 qubits once at the end of the final month → 10 features.
  • QR2 uses inputs RV, MKT, STR, RV_q, EP, INF, DEF and reads all 10 qubits at two times (two "virtual nodes") during the final month → 20 features, requiring two complete circuit executions.
  • Forecasts are scored from January 2018 to August 2026 (104 months), the "extended" out-of-sample period, using rolling training windows of 120 months and 571 months. Stochastic models (QR1, QR2, CRL, CRLX, LSTM, LSTMX) are run with five seeds (0–4).
  • All quantum results are ideal, noise-free local simulations. Nothing here measures IonQ hardware performance.

Part A — Circuit design

Figure 1. Circuit protocol for one forecast

Figure 1. Qubits q0–q6 are input qubits and q7–q9 are memory qubits; memory starts in |000⟩ for every forecast. Each month's seven inputs are loaded with RY(πx) rotations (blue), the whole register evolves under U(τ) with XX couplings and Z fields (purple), and the input qubits are then reset (orange) before the next month is loaded. This repeats for months t−3, t−2 and t−1; in the final month the evolution is applied in V slices dU(τ/V) up to readout endpoint v, and all qubits are measured in Z. QR1 has one endpoint; QR2 has two and therefore needs one complete run per endpoint. Backend support for the mid-circuit resets has not been verified.

PDF · Data 1 · Data 2 · Data 3

Figure 2. Gate sequence for one month

Figure 2. Gate-level view of one month. RY(πx) encodes each input on q0–q6. One Trotter step then applies 45 RXX gates (one per qubit pair, angle 2JijΔt) followed by RZ(2Δt) on all 10 qubits; this block repeats n times to approximate U(τ). Measurement (M) happens only at the final readout, because measuring earlier would destroy the memory.

Part B — Data and inputs

Figure 3. Volatility target series

Figure 3. The forecasting target over 920 monthly observations (January 1950 – August 2026). Top left: log RV for the full history, with the 2018–2026 extension shaded. Top right: the extension in RV units, showing the March 2020 COVID spike (~0.27) and the April 2025 spike (~0.14). Bottom left: histograms of log RV for 1950–2017 vs. 2018–2026; the recent period sits slightly higher. Bottom right: autocorrelation at lags 1–24 months. Historical persistence decays slowly (0.70 at lag 1, still ~0.12 at lag 24), while 2018–2026 drops to near zero by lag 4, so the recent past is a weaker guide to the next month.

Figure 4. Missing data

Figure 4. Left: missing cells per variable in the raw extension (orange) versus the prepared snapshot (teal). MKT, SMB, HML and STR were each missing for all 104 extension months (416 cells); preparation recovered 412 from the Kenneth French data library. Right: remaining gaps by month (black = missing). Only August 2026 values of MKT, SMB, HML and STR are still missing, so September 2026 forecasts that need them cannot be produced.

Figure 5. Input encoding angles

Figure 5. Distribution of each input's RY rotation angle (π × normalized value) for 1950–2017 (teal) and 2018–2026 (orange); dotted lines mark the historical minimum and maximum angle. Most inputs stay within their historical range. Four DP values fall just below the historical minimum and two IP values (including a −0.41 rad outlier) fall below theirs; these were not clipped. DP and EP are concentrated in a much narrower band than historically, so they vary little in the recent period.

Figure 6. Input correlations by period

Figure 6. Pearson correlation between every pair of the nine quantum inputs, 1950–2017 (left) and 2018–2026 (right). Red = move together, blue = move oppositely. DP and EP are strongly correlated historically (0.87). In the recent period DP–DEF becomes strongly positive (0.80) while DP–EP weakens (0.47), and DP–INF turns negative, so relationships learned from history may not hold.

Figure 7. Qubit coupling matrices

Figure 7. Coupling strength Jij between each pair of the 10 qubits (brighter = stronger, range 0–~0.23). Left: the seed-0 matrix used for both QR models in the extended study. Middle and right: the original author matrices for QR1 and QR2. White lines separate input qubits (0–6) from memory qubits (7–9). Part C — Reservoir outputs

Figure 8. Quantum output (feature) traces

Figure 8. Heat map of every feature (rows) by target month (columns), 2018–2026, seed 0. Each cell is a qubit's Z expectation value (−1 blue to +1 red). Labels read vk_qn: readout endpoint k, qubit n. Input-qubit rows (q0–q6) change month to month with the data; memory-qubit rows (q7–q9) and some inputs (QR1 q3, QR2 q5) are nearly constant. In QR2 the v1 and v2 rows look almost identical, so the second readout repeats much of the first.

PDF · Data 1 · Data 2

Figure 9. Feature variance

Figure 9. Variance of each feature over the full valid history, on a log scale. Most input-qubit features vary by ~0.03–0.2, but memory features (q7–q9) vary by only ~0.0002–0.0006, and the least-variable features (QR1 v1_q3: 0.000081; QR2 v1_q5: 0.000024) are about 1,000× smaller. Features this flat would be hard to measure above shot noise (see Figure 21).

PDF · Data

Figure 10. Feature correlations

Figure 10. Pearson correlation between every pair of features for QR1 (10 × 10) and QR2 (20 × 20). The three memory-qubit features (q7–q9) are strongly correlated with each other. In QR2, each v1 feature is almost perfectly correlated with the same qubit's v2 feature (the bright off-diagonal stripe, ~0.99), confirming that the second readout adds little. Removing outputs or qubits would still need to be tested on forecast accuracy.

PDF · Data 1 · Data 2

Figure 11. Feature singular-value spectra

Figure 11. Singular values of the pre-2018 feature matrix, each divided by the largest, for raw features and for centered/standardized features. A steep drop means some feature directions are nearly duplicates. QR1's raw spectrum falls to ~0.001 by the 10th value; QR2's falls to ~0.0002 by the 20th, with a sharp drop after the 8th, so roughly half of QR2's 20 features add little independent information.

PDF · Data

Figure 12. Readout conditioning

Figure 12. Condition number of the training feature matrix at each forecast month (log scale), for 120-month (left) and 571-month (right) training windows. Higher means the fitted readout is more sensitive to small errors in the features. Median values: QR1 ≈ 967 vs. QR2 ≈ 5,982 (120 months); QR1 ≈ 777 vs. QR2 ≈ 4,723 (571 months). QR2 is about six times more sensitive under both windows.

PDF · Data 1 · Data 2

Figure 13. Memory-state purity

Figure 13. Purity of the 3-qubit memory state after 0–3 monthly inputs, for 12 evenly spaced example forecasts (one line each). Purity starts at 1 (fresh memory) and falls to an average of 0.509 (QR1) and 0.484 (QR2) after three months; the dotted line is the minimum possible value, 0.125 (maximally mixed). Mixing happens even without hardware noise, because memory becomes entangled with input qubits that are then reset. Purity alone does not show whether the memory is useful.

Part D — Forecast performance

Figure 14. Forecasts versus observed volatility

Figure 14. Observed log RV (black) and one-month-ahead forecasts (color) for QR1 (top) and QR2 (bottom), with 120-month (left) and 571-month (right) training windows, 2018–2026. The bold line is seed 0; faint lines are seeds 1–4. Forecasts follow the general level but lag or miss sudden spikes (March 2020, April 2025). The 120-month QR1 model shows one large overshoot in mid-2020. Faint lines show seed variation, not confidence intervals.

PDF · Data

Figure 15. Forecast errors over time

Figure 15. Monthly forecast error (predicted − observed log RV) for each model and window; the horizontal line is zero error, and each line is one seed. Above zero means the forecast was too high. The largest errors cluster around 2020: a ≈ −1.7 underprediction when volatility jumped in March 2020, followed (120-month QR1) by a ≈ +2.6 overprediction after it fell. The 571-month window gives smaller seed-to-seed spread than the 120-month window.

PDF · Data

Figure 16. Error distribution and autocorrelation

Figure 16. Left: histograms of forecast errors pooled across all five seeds, for each window. Errors are centered near zero but have long tails, especially toward underprediction (left), and a few very large positive errors for 120-month QR1. Right: autocorrelation of errors at lags 1–12 months (line = mean across seeds, shading = range across seeds). Values reach about ±0.15–0.30 at lags 4, 7–8 and 11–12, so errors partly repeat over time. Shading is seed variation, not a confidence interval.

Figure 17. Rolling 12-month error

Figure 17. Mean squared error of log RV over the trailing 12 months, for QR1, QR2, HAR and Persistence (no-change forecast), 2019–2026. All models peak in 2020–2021 (up to ~0.73 for 120-month QR1). The ranking changes over time: with 120 months, QR2 is worst in 2022–2023, while with 571 months QR2 is lowest in 2025–2026. Neither quantum model consistently beats HAR.

PDF · Data

Figure 18. Error by volatility regime

Figure 18. Mean squared log-RV error by volatility regime, for HAR, Persistence, QR1 and QR2. Regimes are low/middle/high thirds of pre-2018 log RV; the 104 test months split into 19 low, 39 middle and 46 high. All models do best in the middle regime (MSE ≈ 0.05–0.11) and worse at the extremes (≈ 0.22–0.38). With 571 months, both QR models beat HAR in high-volatility months (≈ 0.237 vs. 0.268); with 120 months they do worse (0.344 and 0.376 vs. 0.303). Months are grouped by the realized outcome, so this is descriptive.

Figure 19. Forecast availability

Figure 19. Number of forecast records per model and window, including the unscored September 2026 month, split into successful (ok), failed and unavailable. Part E — Running on hardware

Figure 20. Trotter accuracy versus gate count

Figure 20. Left: mean (solid) and maximum (dashed) absolute error in Z expectation between the Trotter approximation and the exact evolution, over 12 histories and every readout, at 1, 2, 4 and 8 Trotter steps. Middle: RXX gates needed for one complete three-month forecast, summed over endpoints. Right: accuracy vs. gate cost. Mean error falls from 0.0704 to 0.0050 (QR1) and 0.0236 to 0.0054 (QR2), while RXX gates rise eightfold (QR1: 135 → 1,080; QR2: 315 → 2,520). These are logical gates, not compiled IonQ counts.

PDF · Data 1 · Data 2 · Data 3

Figure 21. Shot-sampling uncertainty

Figure 21. Standard error of each measured Z expectation as a function of shots per endpoint (log–log). Solid: median across features; dashed: largest; dotted: the worst-case bound 1/√shots. Worst-case error is 0.10, 0.032 and 0.01 at 100, 1,000 and 10,000 shots (median ≈ 0.069, 0.022, 0.007). Even 0.01 is far larger than the ~0.005–0.024 standard deviation of the memory features in Figure 9. This is ideal sampling noise only; real hardware noise would add to it.

Results

Headline forecast results (from the 24 September 2026 extended study)

MSE of log RV for the extended paper-feature protocol. Lower is better. Bold marks the lowest value in each row among the three listed models.

Period Window Best model overall Best MSE Best RMSE HAR MSE QR1 MSE QR2 MSE
Last 12 months (Sep 2025–Aug 2026) 120 HARX 0.0638 0.253 0.0902 0.1045 0.1234
Last 12 months (Sep 2025–Aug 2026) 571 HARX 0.0639 0.253 0.0855 0.0828 0.0727

Full test (Jan 2018–Aug 2026) 571 HARX 0.1711 0.414 0.1871 0.1802 0.1737

Reading the table: a classical model is best in every row. Over the full test with the 571-month window, both QR models beat HAR but not HARX. With the 120-month window, both QR models are worse than HAR. The 95% Model Confidence Set retains both QR models alongside most classical models in every setting, so these differences are not statistically decisive.

Definitions of metrics and terms

Results-table columns

Term Definition Better is
Protocol Which data and feature set the models use. Extended paper features: the original paper's inputs extended to 2026 (reported here). Modern price features: an independently rebuilt dataset from price data; its target differs slightly, so its scores are not compared directly with this one. —
Period The months scored. Full test / post2017: January 2018 – August 2026 (104 months). Last 12 / last12: September 2025 – August 2026. —
Window Length of the rolling training window: the model is refit each month on the most recent 120 months (10 years) or 571 months (~47.5 years). Shorter adapts faster; longer is more stable. Neither; both are reported without choosing after the fact
Best model overall Model with the lowest MSE among all 12 for that row. —
MSE (mean squared error) Average of (predicted − observed log RV)² over the scored months. Squaring makes big misses count heavily. Lower
RMSE (root mean squared error) √MSE, in log-RV units. An RMSE of 0.25 means forecasts are typically off by about 25% in volatility terms. Lower
HAR / QR1 / QR2 MSE MSE of those specific models, shown for comparison. HAR is the standard volatility benchmark. Seeded models are averaged over five seeds. Lower
QLIKE Alternative loss computed on variance (RV²) rather than log RV. It penalizes underpredicting volatility more than overpredicting, which matters for risk management. Lower
Model Confidence Set (MCS), 95% Statistical test that keeps every model that cannot be ruled out as the best at 95% confidence (10,000 bootstrap replications, 6-month blocks). A large set means the data cannot separate the models. Being retained is good; a small set is more decisive
Seeds Repeated runs of a random model with different random settings (couplings, initial weights). They show sensitivity to luck, not extra market data. Smaller spread across seeds
Scored / unscored Scored forecasts have an observed target to compare against. September 2026 has no observed target yet, so it is unscored. —
Failed / unavailable Failed: the model fit crashed numerically. Unavailable: required inputs were missing. Both are excluded from scoring. Lower

Models

Model Description
Persistence Forecasts next month's volatility as equal to this month's. The simplest possible benchmark.
AR1 / AR3 Autoregression: linear model on the last 1 or 3 months of log RV.
HAR Heterogeneous autoregressive model: linear model on average volatility over the last 1, 3 and 12 months. The standard volatility benchmark.
HARX HAR plus 10 macro predictors (MKT, ΔDP, IP, DEF, EP, SMB, ΔTB, HML, INF, STR).
ARMAX AR(3) plus the same 10 macro predictors.
CRL / CRLX Classical reservoir (echo-state network). CRL uses RV only (50 neurons); CRLX uses RV plus 10 macro inputs (20 neurons).
LSTM / LSTMX Long short-term memory neural networks. LSTM uses RV only; LSTMX uses 11 inputs.
QR1 Quantum reservoir, 10 qubits, one readout endpoint (10 features).
QR2 Quantum reservoir, 10 qubits, two readout endpoints (20 features), different input set from QR1.

Input variables

Variable Meaning
RV Realized volatility of the S&P 500 in the month (normalized). Also the forecasting target, as log RV.
RV_q Average of the previous 3 months of RV ("quarterly"), normalized.
RV_a, RV1, RV2 12-month average RV, and RV lagged 1 and 2 months (used by classical models).
MKT Market excess return (Fama-French market factor).
SMB, HML Fama-French size (small minus big) and value (high minus low book-to-market) factors.
STR Fama-French short-term reversal factor (last month's losers minus winners).
DP Dividend-price ratio (dividend yield) of the market.
EP Earnings-price ratio of the market.
IP Industrial production growth.
INF Monthly US inflation rate.
DEF Default spread: yield gap between lower- and higher-rated corporate bonds, a credit-risk proxy.
TB Treasury bill rate.
Extended period January 2018 – August 2026, added beyond the original paper's data; compared against 1950–2017 ("historical").

Circuit and reservoir terms

Term Definition Better is
Qubit Quantum bit. q0–q6 hold inputs; q7–q9 hold memory. Fewer is cheaper and less noisy, if accuracy holds
Memory qubits The 3 qubits that are never reset during a forecast, so they carry information from earlier months. —
Reset Returns input qubits to 0⟩ between months so new data can be loaded.
Encoding angle (RY(πx)) Each normalized input x rotates its qubit by π·x radians. Inside the historical range; out-of-range values mean extrapolation
RY, RZ, RXX Gates. RY and RZ rotate one qubit about the Y or Z axis; RXX entangles a pair of qubits. Fewer gates
Coupling Jij Interaction strength between qubits i and j, set randomly by the seed and fixed. Sets the RXX angle 2JijΔt. Neither; a design setting
U(τ), evolution time τ The ideal evolution applied each month, with total time τ. —
Trotter step (n, Δt) One RXX layer plus one RZ layer, approximating a slice Δt of U(τ). More steps are more accurate but cost more gates. Fewest steps with acceptable error
Endpoint / virtual node (v, V) A time within the final month's evolution at which all qubits are read. QR1 has V = 1, QR2 has V = 2. Each endpoint needs its own run. Fewer, unless extra endpoints add information
Z expectation (feature) Average measured value of a qubit, from −1 to +1. Named vk_qn (endpoint k, qubit n). These are the inputs to the trained readout. The level is not scored; more variation over time is better
Readout The linear model trained on the features to produce the forecast. The only trained part of a reservoir. —
Feature variance How much a feature changes across months. Higher; near-zero means almost no signal
Feature correlation Pearson correlation between two features, −1 to +1. Closer to 0; near ±1 means duplicates
Singular values (relative) Size of each independent direction in the feature matrix, divided by the largest. Larger and more even; tiny values mean redundancy
Condition number Largest ÷ smallest singular value of the training feature matrix; how much small feature errors can be amplified in the fitted readout. Lower
Purity (hidden-state purity) Tr(ρ²) of the 3-qubit memory state; 1 = pure, 0.125 = maximally mixed. Neither on its own
Logical gate count Gates in the abstract circuit before compiling to a specific machine. Lower
Circuit depth Number of sequential gate layers; deeper circuits take longer and accumulate more hardware error. Lower
Trotter / Z-expectation error Absolute difference between Trotterized and exact Z expectations. Lower

Error and statistics terms

Term Definition Better is
Log RV Natural logarithm of realized volatility; the scale on which forecasts are made and scored. —
Residual / error Predicted − observed log RV. Positive = overprediction. Closer to 0
Rolling 12-month MSE MSE over the trailing 12 months at each date. Lower
Autocorrelation Correlation of a series with itself k months earlier (lag k). For RV, higher means more forecastable. For errors, nonzero means repeated mistakes. RV: higher. Errors: near 0
Lag Number of months back being compared. —
Regime (low / middle / high) Months grouped by realized log RV using the thirds of the pre-2018 distribution. Lower error in each, and similar across them
Shots Number of times the circuit is run to estimate each Z expectation. More is more precise but costs more
Shot standard error (SE) Sampling uncertainty of a Z expectation: √((1 − ⟨Z⟩²)/shots), at most 1/√shots. Lower, and well below the feature's own variation
Median / largest marginal SE SE across all features, summarized by its median and maximum. Lower
Missing cells Data values with no observation. Lower

Bottom line

  • No quantum advantage is established. A classical model (HARX or AR1) is best in every headline setting, and the confidence sets keep the quantum models alongside most classical ones. QR models beat HAR only with the 571-month window.
  • Many quantum features are redundant or nearly constant. Memory features barely vary, QR2's second readout nearly duplicates the first, and QR2's readout is about six times worse conditioned than QR1's.
  • Hardware feasibility is unproven. The flattest features vary less than shot noise even at 10,000 shots, compiled gate counts and mid-circuit reset support on IonQ are unknown, and QR2 needs twice the executions.
  • Data caveats. The 2018–2026 period has weaker volatility persistence, shifted input correlations and a few out-of-range DP and IP values, and August 2026 factor data are still missing.
